5220:
To encipher something means to take a readable message and deliberately scramble or transform it — following a specific set of rules — so that it becomes unreadable to anyone who doesn't know how to reverse the transformation. The goal is always secrecy.

Think of it this way: you have a normal message that anyone could read. You run it through a secret process. What comes out the other side looks like gibberish. That process of converting your readable message into that gibberish is called enciphering.
Two Key Terms You Need to Know First

To fully understand "encipher," you need to know two words that are always involved:

Plaintext — the original, readable message. The thing you start with. It's called "plain" because it is open and clear: anyone who sees it understands it.

Ciphertext — the scrambled, unreadable result after you have enciphered the plaintext. It looks like nonsense to anyone who doesn't have the secret key.

So: encipher is the action of turning plaintext → ciphertext.

A cipher is the specific system of rules you use to do the scrambling. It is a defined algorithm — a step-by-step method — that transforms each character (a letter, a digit, a symbol) of the original message in a predictable way, based on a secret key. The cipher is the engine, and the key is what makes your engine different from everyone else's.

Without the key, even knowing the cipher exists does not help you read the message.
A Simple Example: The Caesar Cipher

The most famous and easy-to-understand cipher is the Caesar cipher. The rule is: shift every letter of your message forward by a fixed number of positions in the alphabet.

Say your key is the number 3 (shift forward by 3):

  • A becomes D
  • B becomes E
  • H becomes K
  • E becomes H
  • L becomes O
  • O becomes R

So if you encipher the word HELLO using this Caesar cipher with a key of 3, you get: KHOOR.

"KHOOR" is meaningless to anyone who stumbles upon it. But your intended reader, who knows the rule (Caesar cipher) and the key (shift of 3), can simply reverse the process and read "HELLO."

That entire act — taking "HELLO" and producing "KHOOR" by applying that rule — is what it means to encipher a message.

The opposite of enciphering is deciphering — taking the ciphertext and reversing the transformation to recover the original plaintext, using the correct key. You cannot decipher a message without knowing the cipher and the key.

Encipher → Decipher. Scramble → Unscramble.

The key is what controls exactly how the cipher scrambles the message. Two people using the same cipher but different keys will produce completely different ciphertext from the same plaintext. The key is secret — it is the critical piece of information that only the sender and the intended receiver should know.

This is why enciphering provides security. Even if an attacker knows which cipher was used, without the key, the ciphertext remains unreadable.

These words are closely related, and understanding the boundaries between them will sharpen your understanding of "encipher":

Encipher vs. Encrypt

In everyday usage and in most modern writing, these two words are used interchangeably, and that is perfectly acceptable. However, in the technical, historical language of cryptography (the science of secret communication), there is a subtle distinction:

  • Encipher is specifically about applying a cipher — a transformation that works at the individual character level, letter by letter or symbol by symbol.
  • Encrypt is the broader term. It covers any method of making information secret, including ciphers but also other approaches. You can say "encrypt" in virtually any context where you'd say "encipher," but "encipher" is slightly more specific.

In practice, especially in modern computing and cybersecurity, "encrypt" is far more commonly used. "Encipher" is the more classical, formal term, but both are correct and understood.

Encipher vs. Encode

These are sometimes confused, and the distinction matters:

  • To encode means to convert information into a different format or representation. Encoding is not necessarily about hiding meaning — it's about changing the form. For example, converting text to Morse code (dots and dashes) is encoding. Converting text to binary (1s and 0s) is encoding. The transformation follows a known, public system, and there is no secret key involved. Anyone who knows the system can reverse it.
  • To encipher is always about hiding meaning through secrecy. A key is involved. The transformation is designed to be unreadable without authorization.

In short: encoding changes form; enciphering hides meaning. An encoded message is not secret — anyone who knows the encoding scheme can read it. An enciphered message is secret — you need the key.
Who Uses This Word and When

You will encounter "encipher" primarily in:

  • Historical and literary contexts: books, films, and articles about wartime intelligence, spies, and secret communications (e.g., WWII-era cipher machines like the Enigma machine enciphered millions of military messages).
  • Cryptography and mathematics: academic and technical writing about classical ciphers and the history of cryptography.
  • Formal or technical writing: security documentation, cryptographic standards, and academic papers may still use "encipher," though "encrypt" is more dominant today.
  • Figurative use: occasionally, "encipher" is used metaphorically to describe making something deliberately obscure or incomprehensible — for example, "his instructions were so convoluted that they might as well have been enciphered." This is informal and less common.

• "Before the courier left, the general enciphered his orders so that even if the message was intercepted, the enemy could not read them."
  • "She enciphered every email she sent to her contact abroad."
  • "The machine enciphered the signal automatically before transmission."
  • "Without knowing the key, you cannot decipher what has been enciphered."
  • "During the Cold War, both sides enciphered their diplomatic cables using highly sophisticated methods."

To summarize everything cleanly:

To encipher is to transform a readable message (plaintext) into an unreadable, scrambled form (ciphertext) by applying a cipher — a specific rule-based transformation — controlled by a secret key. The purpose is always to hide the meaning of the message from unauthorized readers. Only someone who possesses the correct key and knows the cipher can reverse the process and recover the original message. The reverse action is called deciphering. In modern usage, "encipher" and "encrypt" are near-synonyms, with "encrypt" being broader and more common today, while "encipher" is the classical, more precise term for character-level cipher-based transformations.
5221:
To encircle something means to go all the way around it, forming a complete ring or circle. When something encircles something else, it surrounds it on every side, leaving no gap or opening.

Think of it this way: imagine drawing a circle on paper around a dot. Your pen goes all the way around — left, right, top, bottom — until it comes back to where it started. That is exactly what encircling means. The dot is trapped inside a complete ring.

The soul of this word is completeness. This is what makes "encircle" special and different from weaker words like "border" or "flank" (which only mean being on one side of something).

To encircle is NOT:

  • To stand next to something ❌
  • To surround it on just two or three sides ❌

To encircle IS:

  • To wrap around something on all sides, with no way in or out ✅

If soldiers surround a fort but leave one side open, they have not encircled it. The moment they close that gap and complete the ring, they have encircled it.

This is when encircle describes something you could actually see with your eyes.

  • "A stone wall encircles the old village."

The wall runs all the way around the village — north, south, east, west — forming a complete boundary.

  • "The army encircled the enemy base."

Soldiers moved into position on every side of the base, surrounding it completely so nobody could escape or get in.

  • "She encircled his wrist with her fingers."

Her fingers wrapped fully around his wrist, like a bracelet, touching on all sides.

  • "The mountains encircle the valley."

The mountains stand on every side of the valley, surrounding it like the walls of a bowl.

In all of these cases, you can picture the ring — the complete, unbroken loop around something.

"Encircle" is also used when talking about things you cannot physically see — feelings, ideas, or atmospheres. Here, it means something grips, envelops, or completely holds something in an emotional or symbolic sense.

  • "Sadness encircled her heart."

Sadness completely surrounded and consumed her emotionally — she could not escape it. It gripped her from every direction.

  • "A sense of mystery encircles the abandoned mansion."

The feeling of mystery is all around the mansion — in its history, its silence, its appearance — completely surrounding it.

  • "Danger encircled the explorers."

Threats were coming from every direction; there was no safe side.

The logic is the same as the literal uses — completeness, surrounding, no escape — but applied to feelings and atmospheres instead of physical things.

You will see this word used in different forms depending on the sentence:

  • Encircles → used for a single subject in the present: "The river encircles the island."
  • Encircled → past tense: "The troops encircled the town overnight."
  • Encircling → ongoing action: "The encircling crowd made her nervous."
  • Encirclement → the noun form (the act or state of being encircled): "The encirclement of the city lasted three weeks."

These words are close in meaning, but not identical:

  • Surround — The closest synonym. You can almost always swap one for the other. The only difference is that "encircle" carries a slightly stronger image of a circular ring, while "surround" is more general. In everyday use, they are nearly identical.
  • Enclose — Means to shut something inside boundaries, but the boundaries don't have to be circular. A square box encloses things; it does not encircle them.
  • Encompass — Means to include or surround, but is used more often in figurative or intellectual senses ("The book encompasses many topics") rather than physical ones.
  • Ring — Used the same way as encircle in many cases ("Trees ringed the lake"), but "ring" is more informal and compact.
  • Hem in — Means to surround and restrict, with emphasis on trapping. It always has a negative connotation of being unable to move freely.

Encircle sits perfectly in the middle — vivid, precise, and usable in both physical and figurative contexts, with a clear image of a complete ring.

Words that mean the opposite of encircle:

  • Free / release — to let something out of a surrounding ring
  • Open up / break through — to create a gap in the circle
A Quick Summary to Lock It In

To encircle = to form a complete, unbroken ring around something or someone, surrounding it on all sides, physically or figuratively.

If you ever see this word and feel unsure, just picture a circle being drawn around something — all the way around, no gaps — and you have understood it perfectly.
5222:
An enclave is a distinct territory, community, or area that is completely — or largely — surrounded by something meaningfully different from itself.

Picture a small island of blue sitting inside a vast sea of red. That blue island, fully enclosed by red, is an enclave. Two things always define it: it is distinct (different in some important way from what surrounds it), and it is enclosed (wrapped on all or most sides by that different thing).

This is the word's most precise and formal use. In geography and international relations, an enclave is a territory or country that is physically enclosed within the borders of another country, yet remains politically separate from it.

Real examples make this very clear:

Lesotho is an entire country sitting completely inside South Africa. If you look at a map, South Africa wraps all the way around Lesotho on every side. Lesotho has its own government, its own laws, its own identity — but geographically, it is trapped inside another country. That makes it a perfect enclave.

Vatican City is a tiny, independent state enclosed entirely within the city of Rome, Italy. Walk in any direction from Vatican City and you immediately enter Italy. Yet Vatican City governs itself completely. It is an enclave inside Italy.

San Marino is yet another sovereign country sitting entirely inside Italy — another enclave.

In each case, the enclosed place is politically and legally separate from the country that physically surrounds it.
A Note on "Exclave" — Its Close Relative

If you ever come across the word exclave, here is how to tell the two apart, because confusing them is very common.

The difference is about perspective — whose eyes you're looking through.

An enclave is the term used from the perspective of the surrounding territory. South Africa would say: "There is an enclave of Lesotho inside our borders."

An exclave is the term used from the perspective of the enclosed territory's own country. If a piece of Country A gets cut off from Country A's main body and ends up surrounded by foreign land, that piece is called an exclave of Country A.

Here's the key insight: a place can be both an enclave and an exclave at the same time. Take Kaliningrad, a region of Russia. It is physically cut off from the main body of Russia by Lithuania and Belarus. Russia calls it an exclave (a separated piece of Russia). The surrounding countries call it an enclave (a patch of Russian territory sitting inside European territory). Both descriptions are correct — they're just from different viewpoints.

But not all enclaves are exclaves. Lesotho is an enclave (as seen from South Africa), but Lesotho is its own fully independent country, not a separated piece of some larger nation. So it is an enclave but not an exclave.

And not all exclaves are enclaves. Alaska is an exclave of the United States — it's physically separated from the rest of the country by Canada. But Alaska is not an enclave, because it's not fully surrounded by one foreign country. It has coastline opening to the ocean, so it isn't truly enclosed.
In Everyday Social and Cultural Life

Beyond formal geography, "enclave" is used all the time in everyday language to describe any tight-knit, distinct community or area that exists inside a larger, different surrounding. This is probably the most common way you'll encounter the word.

Ethnic enclaves are neighborhoods in big cities where immigrant communities have clustered together, preserving their language, food, customs, and culture. Chinatown in San Francisco or Little Italy in New York are famous examples. These neighborhoods feel culturally distinct from the rest of the city around them — they are enclaves of a specific culture within the broader, diverse city.

Wealthy enclaves — A gated community of very wealthy families sitting inside an otherwise working-class city is often called "a wealthy enclave." The area is economically and socially distinct from everything surrounding it.

Ideological enclaves — You might hear: "That city is a liberal enclave in an otherwise conservative state," or "That rural county is a conservative enclave in a liberal region." This means: a concentrated pocket of people with one set of beliefs, surrounded by people who mostly believe something different.

Professional or industrial enclaves — Silicon Valley is sometimes called an enclave of the technology industry: a dense, self-contained concentration of one kind of world sitting within the broader world.

In every case, the logic is the same as in geography — something distinct, surrounded by something different.
The Tone and Feeling the Word Carries

"Enclave" carries a subtle sense of separateness and self-containment. It suggests that the enclosed place exists as its own little world — maintaining its identity, its character, its way of life — even while being surrounded by something completely different. There's always the implication of contrast: the enclave is not like what's outside it.

The word is neutral on its own, but context can give it different shades:

It can feel positive — "a beautifully preserved cultural enclave that has kept its traditions alive for generations" — suggesting resilience and richness.

It can feel negative or isolating — "the executives lived in a privileged enclave, completely disconnected from ordinary people" — suggesting insularity or elitism.

Or it can be purely descriptive — "the Vatican is an enclave within Italy" — with no emotional charge at all.

An enclave is a distinct place, community, or area — whether a whole country or just a neighborhood — that is surrounded by and noticeably different from whatever lies outside it. It is a world unto itself, enclosed within a larger, different world.
5223:
To enclose something means to surround it completely on all sides, or to place it inside something else so that it is contained within it. Both ideas share the same heart: a boundary is created, and something ends up inside that boundary.

The word has two distinct but closely related senses. Understanding both will give you full command of this word.
Sense 1 — To surround something completely, shutting it in

When you enclose something in this sense, you create a complete boundary around it — not a partial wall, but a full, closed-off barrier. The key is completeness. Something that is enclosed has no open side; it is wrapped, ringed, or bordered on all sides.

Examples:

  • The farmer built a fence to enclose his cattle. — The fence runs all the way around, so the cattle cannot wander out.
  • The courtyard was enclosed by tall stone walls. — You cannot enter or leave except through a gate; every side is sealed.
  • Mountains enclose the valley on three sides, making it feel like a hidden world.
  • The cocoon encloses the caterpillar while it transforms.

Notice what makes "enclose" precise here: it isn't just near something or partially around it. To enclose is to fully wrap something within a boundary, separating it from the open space outside.

This sense is why you'll often hear "enclosed space" in safety contexts — an enclosed parking garage, an enclosed room with no windows, an enclosed mine shaft. These are spaces where the complete surrounding creates concerns about air quality or escape routes.
Sense 2 — To put something inside an envelope or package along with something else

This is the everyday, practical sense you will encounter constantly in letters, emails, and formal writing. When you enclose something in a letter or package, you are physically placing it inside alongside the main item — tucking it in, so to speak.

Examples:

  • I am enclosing a copy of my resume with this application. — The resume is physically inside the same envelope as the letter.
  • Please find the cheque enclosed. — A very common phrase in formal letters, meaning: "I've put the cheque inside this envelope for you."
  • She enclosed a photograph in the birthday card.
  • He enclosed the signed contract and mailed it back.

You will frequently see the phrases "please find enclosed..." or "enclosed herewith..." in formal business or official letters. These are simply polished ways of saying: "I have included the following item inside this envelope/package."

They share the exact same logic. In Sense 1, the boundary is physical and large — walls, fences, mountains forming a closed space. In Sense 2, the boundary is an envelope or package — a smaller physical container. In both cases, something is placed inside a complete boundary, separated from the outside. The word just scales up and down depending on context.
The Nuance and Feel of the Word

"Enclose" carries a quiet sense of containment — and depending on context, this containment can feel protective, restrictive, or simply organizational.

  • Protective: A mother's arms enclose her child. The hard shell encloses the seed, keeping it safe.
  • Restrictive: High prison walls enclose the inmates.
  • Organizational: An envelope encloses documents for neat, safe delivery.

The word itself is neutral — it doesn't judge whether being enclosed is good or bad. Context does that work for you.
Related Word Forms You Should Know

Enclosed (adjective) — Used to describe a space that is fully surrounded, or an item that has been included in an envelope or package.

  • It was an enclosed garden, sheltered from the wind by tall hedges. (surrounded space)
  • Please sign and return the enclosed form. (the form that is inside this envelope)

Enclosure (noun) — Has two meanings mirroring the two senses above:

  1. A surrounded, fenced-in area. The zoo built a larger enclosure for the elephants.
  2. Something included inside a letter or package. The application had two enclosures: a passport photo and a signed declaration.

Surround vs. Enclose — "Surround" is broader and doesn't always imply a complete, sealed barrier. Police can surround a building while still leaving some exits open. But a fence encloses a field because it forms a complete, unbroken boundary. Think of "enclose" as a stricter, more complete version of "surround."

Include vs. Enclose — "Include" simply means something is part of a group or set. You include an item on a list. You enclose a document in an envelope — meaning you physically place it inside a container. "Enclose" is always about physically putting something inside something else; "include" doesn't carry that physical sense.

Contain vs. Enclose — A jar contains water, but we wouldn't say the jar encloses the water. "Enclose" stresses the act of surrounding and closing off on all sides; "contain" simply means something is held inside, without necessarily emphasizing the boundary or the act of shutting in.

Confine vs. Enclose — "Confine" means to restrict something to a limited space and almost always carries a negative tone of restriction or imprisonment. "Enclose" is neutral — it simply describes the physical reality of being within a boundary, without judging it.
A Quick Mental Image to Lock This In

Picture a letter on a desk. You fold it, place it in an envelope, add a cheque and a signed form, and seal the envelope. You have just enclosed the documents — they are now inside a complete boundary. Now zoom out: the same logic applies to a garden surrounded by a fence, a valley ringed by mountains, or an animal in a zoo pen. Something is always inside a complete boundary, separated from the open world around it. That is "enclose."
5224:
At the heart of every meaning of enclosure is one simple idea: something is closed in, or shut within a boundary.

Think of the word "enclose" — to close something inside, to surround it, to fence it off. An enclosure is either the result of that action, the space it creates, or the thing that was placed inside. Keep this core idea in mind, and all the meanings will feel natural.
Meaning 1: A Bounded, Enclosed Area or Space

This is the most common meaning. An enclosure is a defined area of land or space that has been surrounded and separated from the outside by walls, fences, hedges, railings, or some other barrier — so that what is inside is kept in, and what is outside is kept out.

The key idea is containment and separation. The barrier draws a clear line between "inside here" and "outside there."

Examples:

  • A zoo has animal enclosures — spaces surrounded by barriers where each species of animal lives. The lions are in one enclosure, the zebras in another.
  • Farmers build enclosures for their livestock — a fenced-off area where cows or sheep can graze without wandering away.
  • Military bases have secure enclosures — walled or fenced perimeters that separate the base from the outside world.
  • Some cricket and horse-racing grounds have a members' enclosure — a specific, roped-off area where only certain people are allowed to stand or sit.

An enclosure doesn't have to be outdoors or large. A pen, a cage, a courtyard surrounded by walls — these are all enclosures. The key quality is that the space is defined and bounded.
Meaning 2: A Document or Item Included with a Letter or Package

This meaning is very different from the first, but it is equally important — especially in formal, official, or business writing.

When you send a letter (especially a formal or professional one) and you include additional documents, papers, photographs, or other items inside the same envelope, those additional items are called enclosures.

The logic is simple: those items have been enclosed — placed inside — along with the letter.

Examples:

  • A job applicant sends a letter to a company. Inside the envelope, they also include their résumé and a copy of their degree certificate. Those two documents are the enclosures.
  • A lawyer sends a letter to a client. Enclosed with the letter is a copy of the signed contract. The contract is the enclosure.
  • A bank sends you a letter, and inside the envelope you also find a new debit card and a leaflet explaining new charges. Both those items are enclosures.

In formal letters, you will often see the word "Enc." or "Encl." written at the bottom, sometimes followed by the names of the enclosed items. This is a standard way of signalling to the reader: "There are additional items inside this envelope — don't miss them."

"Enc: CV, Cover Letter, Two Reference Letters"

In some contexts, especially in legal and official writing, a single enclosed item is also called an enclosure:

"Please sign and return the enclosure." — meaning: sign and return the document that was included with this letter.
Meaning 3: The Act or Process of Enclosing

Enclosure can also refer to the action itself — the act of surrounding something, fencing something off, or shutting something within a boundary. This is a more abstract use of the word.

Examples:

  • "The enclosure of the garden with a brick wall took three weeks." — meaning: the process of surrounding the garden with a wall.
  • "The enclosure of the land by the landlord left the villagers with nowhere to graze their animals." — meaning: the act of fencing off the land.

This use is less common in everyday speech but appears in formal writing, history, and academic contexts.
Meaning 4: The Barrier or Structure Itself

Sometimes the word enclosure refers not to the space inside, but to the physical barrier — the fence, wall, or structure — that creates the enclosed area. This is a narrower use, and it overlaps with Meaning 1, but the emphasis here is on the boundary itself rather than the space it contains.

Example:

  • "Workers repaired the damaged enclosure after the storm." — here, enclosure refers to the fence or wall that was damaged, not the space inside it.

Even though these meanings seem different on the surface, they all come from the same root idea:

MeaningWhat is "enclosed"?
A bounded spaceLand or area is closed off by a barrier
A document in a letterAn item is closed inside an envelope
The act of enclosingThe process of closing something in
The barrier itselfThe structure that does the closing in

Every use of the word circles back to the idea of closing something within a boundary.

1. Enclosures can be permanent or temporary.
A stone wall around a farm has been there for centuries — that's a permanent enclosure. A temporary rope barrier set up at an outdoor concert to create a VIP area is also an enclosure, just not a lasting one.

2. An enclosure implies purpose.
An enclosure isn't just any fenced-off space — it usually exists for a reason: to protect something, to contain something, to keep something separate, or to designate a specific area for a specific use. The word carries a sense of deliberate action.

3. Size doesn't matter.
An enclosure can be as small as a glass tank (a terrarium for a reptile is its enclosure) or as large as a military compound or an entire fenced district. What makes something an enclosure is the idea of a defined, bounded space — not its size.

4. In formal letters, enclosures are distinct from attachments.
In the physical, paper-letter world, an enclosure is something placed inside the same envelope. In email, the equivalent concept is an attachment — a digital file attached to the email. However, in very formal email correspondence (especially legal or official emails), some people still use the word "enclosure" or "Enc." to refer to attached files, carrying over the old letter-writing convention.

5. The word can be used figuratively.
Though less common, enclosure can describe situations where someone feels trapped or confined — not physically, but emotionally or socially. "She felt like she was living in an enclosure" could suggest she felt boxed in, unable to move freely through life. This figurative use is rare and context-dependent.
A Brief Historical Note (Important, Not Just Trivia)

In British history, the word enclosure (often capitalised as Enclosure or used in the phrase the Enclosures) refers to a specific and important historical process that took place mainly between the 16th and 19th centuries. Common land — land that was traditionally shared by the villagers of a community for farming and grazing — was fenced off and turned into private property, often by wealthy landowners. The people who had depended on that shared land lost access to it. The Enclosure Acts were the laws that made this legal.

This historical meaning is significant because you will encounter it frequently in books, articles, and discussions about British and agricultural history. When you see "enclosure" in that context, it refers to the fencing-off of formerly shared land and the social disruption it caused.

Enclosure (noun) means:

  1. A bounded, enclosed area — a space surrounded by a barrier (wall, fence, etc.) to contain or separate what is inside. (A zoo enclosure, a livestock enclosure, a members' enclosure.)
  2. A document or item included in a letter or package — something placed inside an envelope along with a letter. (Signalled by "Enc." at the bottom of formal letters.)
  3. The act of enclosing — the process of surrounding or fencing something off.
  4. The barrier itself — the fence, wall, or structure that creates the enclosed space.
  5. (Historical) The Enclosures — the fencing-off of common land in British history.

The thread running through all of these is always the same: something closed in, bounded, or contained within a defined limit.
5225:
To encode something means to convert it from one form into another form by following a specific set of rules — so that the information can be stored, transmitted, processed, or understood in a particular way.

You start with information in its original form. You apply a set of rules. You end up with the same information expressed in a new form. That whole process is called encoding.

The rules you follow are called the encoding scheme or encoding system. Both the person (or machine) doing the encoding and the one receiving it need to know the same scheme — because whatever is encoded must eventually be decoded to be useful again.

Encoding happens for several reasons:

  • To make information compatible with a specific system (a computer, a network, a device)
  • To compress it so it takes up less space or travels faster
  • To convert it from one medium to another (e.g., sound waves into digital data)
  • To express it in a different symbol system that another party can read
  • To structure it in a way that preserves its meaning through a transformation

Notice: encoding is not necessarily about hiding information. It's about converting it into a usable or compatible form.

Because the idea of "converting information from one form into another by a set of rules" is so universal, the word is used in many very different contexts. Here is a tour of the most important ones:

Computing and Technology

When you type a letter and save it, your computer encodes that letter as a number. The letter "A" is encoded as the number 65 in a system called ASCII. A more modern system called UTF-8 encodes thousands of characters — including letters from every language — into sequences of numbers that machines can store and read. The text you're reading right now exists in your device's memory in encoded form.

When you watch a video online, that video has been encoded into a compressed digital format (such as H.264 or MP4). The raw footage — which would be enormous in size — is encoded into a much smaller file without losing noticeable quality, making it practical to stream over the internet.

Audio and Images

When a microphone captures your voice, the sound waves (which are physical vibrations in air) are encoded into digital data — a sequence of numbers representing the shape of the sound wave at thousands of moments per second. This encoded data can then be stored as an MP3 or WAV file.

Similarly, a camera's sensor captures light and encodes it into digital image data (JPEG, PNG, etc.). Real-world phenomena become numbers that machines can store, copy, and transmit perfectly.

Data Transmission and Networking

When information travels across a network, it's encoded into binary signals — sequences of 0s and 1s — that can move as electrical pulses through cables, or as light pulses through fibre optic lines, or as radio waves through the air. The receiving device decodes those signals back into the original information. Without encoding into a form that can physically travel, no information could cross any distance electronically.

Genetics and Biology

Scientists say a gene "encodes" a protein. This means the sequence of chemical units along a strand of DNA contains the instructions — the code — for building a particular protein. The DNA doesn't look like the protein at all, but it carries the information in a form that the cell's machinery can read and use to construct the protein. The gene is the encoded form; the protein is the result of decoding and executing those instructions.

Linguistics and Communication

When you want to express a thought, you encode it into language. You convert your internal idea into words, sentence structure, tone, and grammar — a form that another person can receive and decode back into meaning. This is one of the oldest and most fundamental uses of the word. The speaker encodes; the listener decodes.

This is also why miscommunication happens: the listener decodes the message differently than the speaker intended. The encoding and decoding didn't match.

Psychology and Memory

When you experience or learn something, your brain encodes it — it converts that experience into a neural pattern that gets stored in memory. Encoding is literally the first step of memory. If information is not successfully encoded, it is never stored. This is why distraction, stress, or poor attention at the moment of learning can prevent memory formation: the encoding step fails.
A Critical Distinction: Encoding Is Not the Same as Encrypting

This is one of the most commonly confused points, so it deserves its own section.

Encoding converts information into a different format using a known, open, publicly available scheme. There is no secret involved. Anyone who knows the scheme can decode it. For example, Base64 is a widely used encoding scheme that converts binary data into a string of readable text characters. It is completely open. Anyone can decode it instantly. No key is needed.

Encryption is specifically and entirely about secrecy. When you encrypt something, you scramble it using a secret key, and without that specific key, it cannot be read — even if you know the encryption algorithm. Encryption is designed to protect information from anyone who doesn't hold the key.

So: encoding is about format conversion and compatibility. Encryption is about secrecy and protection.

You can absolutely encode something without hiding it at all. Base64-encoding an email attachment makes it compatible with email systems — it doesn't make it secret. Anyone can decode it. On the other hand, encrypting a file makes it secret — even if someone intercepts it, they cannot read it without the key.

Using "encode" when you mean "encrypt" is a common mistake. They are related in that both involve transforming information, but their purposes are completely different.

Another important nuance: encoding can either preserve all the original information, or deliberately discard some of it.

Lossless encoding means no information is lost. You can perfectly reconstruct the original from the encoded form. A ZIP file, for example, compresses data losslessly — unzipping it gives you back the exact original. A PNG image is also losslessly encoded.

Lossy encoding means some information is deliberately thrown away, usually to make the file much smaller. An MP3 audio file, for instance, discards sound frequencies that human ears are poor at detecting. A JPEG image discards fine detail that the eye barely notices. You can never perfectly reconstruct the original from a lossy encoding — but the result is often indistinguishable from the original in everyday use, and the file can be ten or twenty times smaller. The tradeoff is compactness in exchange for a small, controlled loss of quality.

It's worth emphasizing: encode and decode are always two halves of the same process.

You encode something at one end. Someone (or something) decodes it at the other end to recover the original meaning or data. This is true in every domain — computers, biology, language, memory. Encoding without decoding is useless; the information exists in a form no one can read.

This is why encoding schemes must be shared or known in advance. If you encode a message using a system the receiver doesn't know, they cannot decode it, and communication fails. The scheme is the shared language of the transformation.

• "The software encodes the raw video footage into a smaller MP4 file before uploading."
  • "DNA encodes the instructions for building every protein in your body."
  • "The brain encodes new experiences into long-term memory during deep sleep."
  • "Please encode the image data in Base64 before sending it through the API."
  • "When we speak, we encode our thoughts into words; the listener decodes them back into meaning."
  • "The message was encoded using a cipher that only the two agents knew."

To encode is to convert information from one form into another form by following a defined set of rules — so that it can be stored, transmitted, processed, or understood — with the understanding that it can be converted back (decoded) by anyone or anything that knows the same rules.
5226: Something is encomiastic when it is full of high, glowing, enthusiastic praise — the kind of praise that doesn't just compliment but lavishes admiration on a person, work, or idea.

There's a difference between saying "that was a good book" and writing a thousand-word tribute calling it "a towering achievement, a gift to humanity, a work that will outlast its generation." The second is encomiastic — it doesn't simply express approval; it heaps it on generously, even grandly.

The word describes a mode of speaking or writing, not just a passing kind word. Encomiastic language feels elevated, warm, and deeply favorable, as though the speaker or writer is actively making a case for how wonderful something is.

It typically describes:

  • A piece of writing — an encomiastic review, an encomiastic biography, an encomiastic essay
  • A speech or remarks — encomiastic tributes at a retirement ceremony, an encomiastic foreword
  • A tone or style — "the encomiastic tone of the article made it feel more like advertising than journalism"
The subtle edge it can carry

Here's an important nuance: while the word itself is neutral, it is often used with a mild critical undertone. Because it signals praise that is unusually high or elaborate, calling something encomiastic can quietly suggest the praise is excessive, one-sided, or uncritical.

For example, if a reviewer says "the biography is thoroughly encomiastic," they may be hinting that it's too dazzled by its subject to be objective — more of a fan tribute than a fair assessment. This critical shade isn't always present, but you should watch for it in context.

• "The director's acceptance speech was met with encomiastic remarks from nearly every critic in the room."

— The critics were heaping effusive praise on him.

  • "Her encomiastic foreword called the economist's ideas 'the most transformative of the century.'"

— She wrote a gushing, highly admiring introduction.

  • "Reviewers noted the documentary's encomiastic treatment of its subject — it never once explored his failures."

— The documentary was so full of praise that it felt biased or one-sided.
How it differs from nearby words

• Complimentary — a broader, lighter word; just means saying something nice. Encomiastic implies more intensity and formality.
  • Laudatory — the closest synonym; both mean "expressing praise." Encomiastic is slightly rarer, more literary, and carries a stronger sense of elaborateness — almost ceremonial praise.
  • Flattering — has a personal, often social flavor; can imply strategic niceness. Encomiastic is more about the content and form of the praise itself.
  • Sycophantic — implies insincere, grovelling praise meant to gain favor. Encomiastic is neutral about sincerity; it just describes the character of the praise, not the motive behind it.
Register and where you'll encounter it

This is a formal, literary word. You'll find it in book reviews, academic literary criticism, journalism, and scholarly essays — not in everyday conversation. Encountering it in a text is a signal that the writer is working at a sophisticated level of prose and critical vocabulary.
If you ever need to recall it quickly: encomiastic = characterized by elaborate, glowing praise — and sometimes implies that praise is perhaps a touch overdone.
5227: An encomium is a formal, elaborate, and enthusiastic piece of praise — spoken or written — for a person, a thing, or an achievement. Think of it not as a quick compliment, but as a full, developed tribute: a speech, an essay, or a passage specifically designed to celebrate and honor something or someone in glowing terms.
What makes it different from an ordinary compliment

If you tell a friend "you did a great job," that is a compliment. But an encomium goes far beyond that. It is sustained (it goes on at length), it is deliberate (carefully crafted, not thrown out casually), and it is elevated in tone (formal, respectful, often eloquent). An encomium doesn't just say someone is great — it argues for their greatness with detail, warmth, and effort.

Imagine a retiring teacher who spent 40 years shaping young minds. At her farewell ceremony, a colleague stands up and delivers a ten-minute speech listing her achievements, describing her character, recalling her impact on students, and honoring her legacy. That speech is an encomium.

An encomium is always positive — there is no such thing as a negative encomium. It is also sincere by nature (unlike flattery, which can be hollow and self-serving). It is aimed at honoring, not merely pleasing. And importantly, it has substance — it gives reasons for the praise rather than just declaring admiration out of nowhere.

It can be delivered as a speech (at a ceremony, award event, or retirement dinner), as written text (a book dedication, a tribute essay, a foreword that praises the author), or even as an entire short work in itself (a poem or essay written solely for the purpose of honoring someone).
Real-life situations where you'd encounter an encomium

• A Nobel Prize acceptance speech where a committee chairman lavishes praise on the winner's life's work.
  • The introduction to a biography where the writer spends several paragraphs honoring the subject before the story begins.
  • A Medal of Honor citation read aloud at a military ceremony.
  • A toast at a wedding that goes well beyond "congratulations" and genuinely celebrates the couple's qualities.
  • A book's preface written by a famous author to honor a lesser-known writer whose work deserves more recognition.

In each of these cases, the praise is not casual, not brief, and not accidental. It is deliberate, warm, and crafted with care. That is the signature of an encomium.
How to use it in sentences

• "The senator's colleagues delivered a moving encomium at his retirement banquet."
  • "The documentary was essentially an encomium to the late architect, celebrating every aspect of his vision."
  • "She was embarrassed by the long encomium her boss gave before handing her the award."
  • "The book's opening pages contain a heartfelt encomium to the author's childhood teacher."

Notice how in each case, "encomium" refers to a full piece of sustained, formal praise — not just a sentence or two.

The plural of encomium has two accepted forms: encomiums (the straightforward English plural) and encomia (the classical plural). Both are correct. In everyday writing, encomiums is more commonly seen.
The tone and register of the word itself

The word "encomium" is formal and literary. You would not use it in casual conversation — saying "that speech was quite an encomium" instantly marks you as someone with a sophisticated vocabulary. It belongs in writing about literature, history, rhetoric, or ceremonies. It is the right word when you want to describe praise that is elevated and deliberate, and when a word like "tribute" or "praise" feels too plain for the weight of what is being described.
One final way to lock it in your memory

Picture a grand hall. Tall ceilings, a polished podium. A distinguished speaker rises, clears their throat, and for several minutes speaks only of one person — their brilliance, their courage, their impact, their legacy. The audience is moved. That moment — that speech — is an encomium. It is praise given its fullest, most dignified form.
5228:
Picture drawing a large circle around a group of things. That circle wraps completely around everything inside it — nothing escapes, nothing is left out. That image is the soul of the word encompass. It means to include or contain a wide range of things within something, in a way that is complete and total, leaving nothing important outside.

The feeling of the word is one of wholeness and full coverage. When something encompasses things, it doesn't just touch on them lightly — it holds them all together, like a single container big enough to fit everything inside.

1. To include a broad range of things (the most common meaning)

This is how you will encounter "encompass" the vast majority of the time. It means that one thing — a subject, a role, a concept, a plan — is broad or complete enough to contain many different things within it.

Examples:

  • "The word 'weather' encompasses rain, wind, snow, heat, and humidity." → All of those things live inside that one concept.
  • "Her job encompasses managing the team, setting budgets, and reporting to the board." → All of those duties fall under her single role.
  • "The new law encompasses all forms of workplace discrimination." → The law is broad enough to cover every type, not just some.
  • "The documentary encompasses everything from the early life of the artist to her final years." → The whole story is captured within it.

Notice that in every case, the thing doing the encompassing is large, broad, or complete enough to hold many diverse things inside itself.

2. To surround or encircle something completely (the more literal, physical meaning)

Less common, but worth knowing. "Encompass" can also describe something that physically wraps around something else on all sides, forming a complete boundary around it.

Examples:

  • "The thick forest encompasses the village." → The forest surrounds the village on all sides, like a ring.
  • "High stone walls once encompassed the ancient city." → The walls formed a complete border around the city.

You will mostly encounter this second meaning in literature, historical writing, or geography. In modern everyday writing, the first meaning is far more dominant.
What Makes It Different from Similar Words

This is crucial. "Encompass" is not just a fancier way to say "include." There is a real difference in meaning.

"Include" is neutral and modest. It points to specific items that are part of something, but it doesn't claim to cover everything.

  • "The tour includes a visit to the museum." → A museum visit is one of the things on the list. There may be other items too.

"Encompass" is broader and stronger. It implies that the full range, or all the important aspects of something, are covered — nothing major is left out.

  • "The tour encompasses culture, history, cuisine, and local traditions." → The tour is broad and complete; it captures the whole experience.

So think of "include" as pointing a finger at individual items, and "encompass" as throwing a wide net over the entire territory.

"Cover" is closer to "encompass" in meaning, and sometimes they can be swapped. But "encompass" carries a stronger sense of totality and deliberateness — it emphasizes that the scope is impressively broad.
The Tone and Register of the Word

"Encompass" is a formal or semi-formal word. It fits naturally in academic papers, professional reports, journalism, formal speeches, and serious nonfiction writing. You would not normally use it in casual conversation — saying "this sandwich encompasses everything I love" would sound oddly stiff.

In everyday speech, people tend to use "include," "cover," or "contain" instead. But in written, professional, or academic contexts, "encompass" is a precise and elegant choice that signals broad, complete coverage.

Getting familiar with these patterns will help you both recognize and use the word naturally:

  • "encompasses a wide range of..." — "The program encompasses a wide range of skills, from writing to public speaking."
  • "encompasses everything from X to Y" — "The exhibit encompasses everything from ancient pottery to modern sculpture."
  • "encompasses all aspects of..." — "True fitness encompasses all aspects of physical and mental health."
  • "broadly/fully encompasses" — "The policy broadly encompasses anyone who works for the company, regardless of their role."

Since you want to know this word completely, it helps to know that "encompassing" is its adjective form and means wide-ranging, broad, or all-inclusive.

  • "She had an all-encompassing knowledge of the subject." → Her knowledge covered every single part of it.
  • "The report took an encompassing view of the crisis." → It looked at the big picture, not just one angle.

"All-encompassing" is a very common and useful compound adjective you will encounter often.

To encompass means to include a full and broad range of things within something, in a way that is total and complete — like a circle that wraps around everything inside it and leaves nothing out. It can also mean, more literally, to physically surround something on all sides. It is a formal word, stronger and more complete-sounding than "include," and it is used when you want to emphasize that the scope of something is impressively wide and thorough. The heart of the word is always the same idea: wholeness, completeness, and nothing left outside the boundary.
5229:
Imagine you draw a circle around something. Everything inside that circle is covered — nothing is left out, nothing escapes. That is the feeling "encompassing" gives you.

When you describe something as encompassing, you are saying it is so wide in its reach, so complete in its coverage, that it takes in everything — every part, every angle, every aspect — all at once, leaving nothing outside.

Think of it as the difference between a spotlight and the sun. A spotlight lights up one narrow area. The sun? It encompasses the entire sky. That total, all-around, nothing-left-out quality is what "encompassing" captures.

If something is encompassing, it:

  • Covers a very wide range — it doesn't deal with just one narrow piece; it stretches across many things or all things.
  • Leaves nothing out — it is complete; there are no gaps.
  • Surrounds or contains entirely — the idea of something being wrapped around, held within, or enclosed is built into the word.

"She gave an encompassing explanation of the topic."
→ Her explanation covered every angle — the causes, the effects, the history, the exceptions. You didn't need to ask follow-up questions. Nothing was left unexplained.

"The new law was encompassing in its scope."
→ The law didn't target just one situation or one group of people. It reached broadly, applying to many situations across many contexts.

"The mountains created an encompassing silence."
→ The silence wasn't just in one corner. It surrounded you completely — above, below, all around. You were inside the silence, enveloped by it.

"The professor offered an encompassing view of human history."
→ He didn't focus only on one era or one part of the world. His perspective took in the whole sweep of human history, from all directions.

"Encompassing" works on two related levels, and understanding both will deepen your feel for the word.

Layer 1 — Figurative (most common use): Something that is thorough, broad, and complete in what it includes or addresses. This is how you'll see the word used most often — in ideas, theories, explanations, descriptions, policies, questions, etc.

"He had an encompassing knowledge of medicine" — he knew medicine broadly and deeply, without obvious gaps.

Layer 2 — Literal/Spatial (less common, more literary): Something that physically surrounds or encloses something else, wrapping around it on all sides.

"The encompassing forest made it impossible to see the sky" — the forest spread around them in every direction, closing them in.

Both meanings share the same soul: total coverage, nothing left outside.
How It Differs from Similar Words

This is where many learners get confused, so let's be precise.

Encompassing vs. Broad:
"Broad" just means wide. A broad road is wide. A broad topic covers many things. But "broad" doesn't guarantee completeness — something can be broad yet still have gaps.
"Encompassing" goes further. It implies everything is included. There are no gaps; nothing slips through.

Encompassing vs. Comprehensive:
These two are very close, and you can often swap them. But there's a subtle difference in feel. "Comprehensive" leans toward thoroughness — going into detail, covering every sub-point carefully. "Encompassing" leans toward total reach — covering the full spread, surrounding the whole territory. A comprehensive report is detailed and complete. An encompassing theory wraps around and accounts for everything.

Encompassing vs. Inclusive:
"Inclusive" focuses on not excluding — making sure different types, groups, or cases are welcome and counted. "Encompassing" is about total coverage of scope — the sheer range of what is included, regardless of exclusion concerns.

You will often see the compound form all-encompassing, and it is worth understanding separately.

Where "encompassing" already suggests wide, complete coverage, all-encompassing pushes this to an absolute. It means literally everything is included — there is nothing, not a single thing, that falls outside it.

"His love for music was all-encompassing" — music touched every part of his life: his mood, his work, his relationships, his identity. Nothing in his life was separate from it.

"The storm created an all-encompassing darkness" — the darkness was total. There was no patch of light anywhere. Everything was swallowed by it.

Use "all-encompassing" when you want to signal that the coverage is absolute, not just very wide. It is the extreme end of the spectrum.

When a writer or speaker chooses "encompassing" over simpler words like "wide" or "big," they are deliberately creating an impression: this thing doesn't just touch many points — it surrounds the whole territory. There is a sense of completeness, of being enclosed within something, of nothing being able to escape its reach.

This is why "encompassing" often appears in formal, academic, or literary writing. It is a word with weight. It tells the reader: don't think of this as partial or selective — think of it as total.
A Quick Feel for Register and Frequency

"Encompassing" is a formal word. You will hear it less often in casual conversation and more often in:

  • Academic writing ("an encompassing theoretical framework")
  • Professional or policy contexts ("an encompassing reform of the tax system")
  • Literary or descriptive writing ("the encompassing silence of the desert night")

If you are speaking casually, you would more naturally say "covers everything" or "really thorough." But in writing or formal speech, "encompassing" gives your language precision and gravity.
Encompassing means: so wide in coverage and so complete in reach that everything relevant — every part, every angle, every aspect — is included, with nothing left outside.
